claims.text: The equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni alloy and the compared equiatomic quaternary and ternary subsets are all single-phase FCC after identical thermomechanical processing.
Local lattice distortion influences stacking-fault energy.
Stacking-fault energy influences activated deformation mechanisms, including dislocation slip, twinning, and martensitic transformation.
Spatially variable local stacking-fault energies can provide a range of stress thresholds for partial-dislocation nucleation, promote strain delocalization, and suppress plastic instability.
The greater chemical complexity of the quinary alloy produces larger local lattice distortions than in its quaternary and ternary subsets.
The quinary alloy has more spatially varied local lattice distortions than its quaternary and ternary subsets.
The larger and more varied lattice distortions in the quinary alloy cause a broader stacking-fault-energy distribution.
Solute-dislocation interactions are responsible for the proposed differences in lattice distortion and stacking-fault-energy distributions among the alloys.
A broader stacking-fault-energy distribution in the quinary alloy enhances solute-dislocation interactions and dislocation pinning.
Enhanced dislocation pinning in the quinary alloy increases its work-hardening capability.
The quaternary and ternary subsets have less pronounced lattice distortions and narrower stacking-fault-energy distributions than the quinary alloy.
Reduced dislocation impediment in the quaternary and ternary subsets causes earlier localization of deformation.
Relative to the quinary baseline, the quaternary and ternary alloys will exhibit lower dislocation pinning.
Relative to the quinary baseline, the quaternary and ternary alloys will exhibit lower work-hardening rates.
Relative to the quinary baseline, the quaternary and ternary alloys will exhibit earlier localized deformation and failure.
The quinary alloy is expected to have the highest work-hardening rate and most delayed failure among the compared alloys.
Using identical strain rate, temperature, stress conditions, and thermomechanical processing is intended to isolate intrinsic microstructural contributions to mechanical response.
Diffraction peak-profile analysis can track microstrain and stacking-fault probability during deformation and use them to estimate stacking-fault energy.
Thermomechanical history can affect short-range order and consequently deformation behavior in chemically complex FCC alloys.
